text: By August 1971, the dam was cracking.
President Richard Nixon took his economic team to Camp David for the weekend,
and on Sunday, August 15, he went on television.
A 90-day freeze on wages and prices, a 10% surcharge on imports,
and the big one, the gold window, was closed.
Foreign governments could no longer swap their dollars for American gold.
Nixon pitched it as a pause, with gold to return once the system was fixed.
So, temporary, right?
It never came back.
By 1973, the major currencies were floating, priced by markets instead of metal.
Which leaves a puzzle.
The dollar lost its last link to gold more than 50 years ago.
You'd expect the world to dump it.
Instead, it became even more central.
Why?
Why? Part of it is oil. In 1974, the US and Saudi Arabia reached an informal understanding.
Saudi oil money flowed into US government bonds, and America offered military support.
No formal treaty ever forced oil into dollars, but oil has mostly traded in dollars ever
since. The bigger reason is a network effect. It's why your whole family ends up on the
same messaging app, including the relative who only sends good morning memes. If every
bank, every exporter, and every central bank already uses dollars, the easiest thing for
you to do is use dollars too.
The numbers are wild.
In April 2025, the dollar was on one side of about 89% of all currency trades, in a
market moving roughly $9.6 trillion a day.
Central banks keep about 57% of their own foreign currency reserves in dollars.
The euro, in second place, sits around 20.
Behind that sits a huge, easy-to-trade market for U.S. government bonds.
When the world gets scared, that's where a lot of its money has traditionally run.
But gold never really left.
Central banks bought more than a thousand tons of it in each of 2022, 2023, and 2024,
and another 863 tons in 2025.
Miss me?
So, why not just go back to gold?
Here's the problem.
them. All the gold ever mined, about 222,600 tons, would fit in a single cube, roughly
22.6 meters, on each side. Tie the world's money to that cube, and money can only grow
as fast as miners can dig. In a crisis, central banks' hands are tied. Many economists argue
that's part of what made the Great Depression so brutal.
So, back to the question we started with. What is your money backed by? Read that British
note again. Today, the Bank of England says its promise mostly means one thing. You can
swap the note for another Bank of England note. What really stands behind it is trust. Trust that
the central bank keeps prices stable. Trust in a government that collects taxes in that currency.
And trust that everyone else will still accept it tomorrow. Gold was a promise you could hold.
Paper is a promise you have to believe. And the moment enough people stop believing,
That's when the mirage disappears.
